findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report to the end of July 2026

findings.detail: Manchester's cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £59.2m by March 2026. The statutory override that currently excludes this deficit from council reserves expires March 2028, placing the council at potential Section 114 notice risk.

findings.detail: Additional HRA reserve drawdown is driven by unanticipated statutory and regulatory obligations including fire safety works from Fire Risk Assessments, damp and mould remediation, disrepair claims, and void pressures. findings.paper_title: Housing Repairs Insourcing and Recommissioning Part A
findings.headline: The insourcing may trigger additional capital borrowing and balance sheet liabilities that will increase financing costs and HRA balances.
findings.detail: The proposal requires mobilisation capital for ICT systems, depot facilities, fleet and infrastructure, plus future investment in building safety, fire safety and compliance works (including compartmentation). Capital expenditure 'may require reprofiling of the approved capital programme, identification of alternative funding sources or additional borrowing'. Additionally, lease arrangements for assets and facilities will be recognised on the HRA balance sheet as right-of-use assets with associated liabilities, driving ongoing depreciation and financing charges.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is about to increase its borrowing, whether that borrowing is intended, and what the structural impact on its balance sheet will be—additional debt service will consume part of the £4.8m cost savings.
findings.figures: Unquantified capital investment requirement; additional depreciation and financing charges from lease liabilities
findings.quote: Where investment cannot be accommodated within existing programme allocations, this may require reprofiling of the approved capital programme, identification of alternative funding sources or additional borrowing. Any increase in borrowing would give rise to additional capital financing and interest costs which would need to be reflected within future HRA Business Plan assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Housing Repairs Insourcing and Recommissioning Part A
findings.headline: Repair demand has risen 16% in five years, and benchmarking suggests the council's responsive repair volumes remain higher than the social housing sector average.
findings.detail: Responsive repair jobs rose from 48,866 in 2021/22 to 56,827 projected for 2026/27. The paper notes that benchmarking by Ark Consultancy indicates 'both the overall volume of responsive repairs and the proportion classified as emergency or same-day responses are higher than comparable levels reported across the social housing sector', suggesting demand-management opportunities through triage and prioritisation review.
findings.matters: Rising repair demand could undermine the cost savings, and a lender needs visibility of whether the demand is being tackled or will absorb the efficiency gains.
findings.figures: 56,827 responsive repair jobs in 26/27 vs 48,866 in 21/22 (16% increase); projected 513 void jobs, 14,192 heating jobs, 14,738 electrical jobs for 26/27
findings.quote: The number of responsive repair jobs has risen significantly in recent years, increasing from 48,866 jobs in 2021/22 to 56,827 projected jobs for 26/27 representing an increase of approximately 16% over the period.

findings.paper_title: Housing Repairs Insourcing and Recommissioning Part A
findings.headline: Insourcing is projected to reduce responsive repairs costs from £13.1m in 2027/28 to £8.3m by Year 5, generating approximately £4.8m in savings over five years.
findings.detail: The business case (developed by Ark Consultancy) quantifies the financial case for insourcing. The savings come from reduced repair volumes, improved operative productivity, and lower reliance on agency staff and subcontractors. The paper notes the current external contract cost is 'unsustainable, having increased significantly in recent years'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see whether the council's plan to close a significant deficit is grounded in realistic cost reduction. £4.8m on a £22.758m deficit is material but not sufficient on its own.
findings.figures: £4.8m cost reduction over 5 years; responsive repairs down from £13.1m to £8.3m by Year 5
findings.quote: the business plan developed by Ark Consultancy forecasts a reduction in annual operating costs of approximately £4.8m over the first five years of operation, with responsive repairs costs reducing from £13.1m in 2027/28 to £8.3m by Year 5

findings.paper_title: Housing Repairs Insourcing and Recommissioning Part A

However, the paper is careful to note that insourcing alone will not resolve the HRA's financial challenges, only provide a more sustainable operating model for longer-term recovery.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's housing service is financially sustainable and what the council's actual recovery trajectory looks like—a £22.758m annual deficit is material.
findings.figures: £22.758m annual HRA deficit
findings.quote: The HRA is currently operating at a significant annual deficit of £22.758m and requires a sustainable recovery plan to align expenditure with available income whilst maintaining adequate reserves.

findings.paper_title: Anti-Poverty Budget Update
findings.headline: Housing Payments demand growing and council spending 205% of government allocation, driven by gap between Local Housing Allowance and actual rents
findings.detail: Manchester spent 205% of its DWP allocation in 2025/26, second-highest in England (only Bedford at 206%). Applications are rising year-on-year (4,341 in 2023/24 to 4,743 in 2024/25). In Q1 2026/27, 42.9% of applications are driven by LHA rate shortfalls vs 39.1% for full 2025/26, showing accelerating pressure. LHA rates have not been increased since April 2024.
findings.matters: The council is materially over-funding government allocations due to housing cost pressures in its area, with demand showing acceleration and no prospect of government LHA rate increases to ease the pressure
findings.figures: 2025/26 expenditure 205% of DWP allocation; Q1 2026/27 LHA-driven applications 42.9% vs 39.1% full year 2025/26; average award private tenants £49.43/week vs £23.31 for council/RSL tenants
findings.quote: In 2025/26, expenditure reached 205% of the DWP allocation, demonstrating a substantial local commitment to supporting residents. This level of expenditure is notably higher than that of most other local authorities, which typically spend at or close to their DWP allocation.

findings.paper_title: Anti-Poverty Budget Update
findings.headline: Council Tax Support costs £42.8m but government funds only £21.8m, leaving a £21m annual unfunded subsidy
findings.detail: The council notionally receives £21.8m from government for Council Tax Support but the actual scheme costs £42.8m to operate. This £21m annual gap is funded from the council's own resources. The document notes this represents a structural pressure as cuts to the Settlement Funding Assessment since 2014 have eroded the notional CTS element while caseload pressures increase.
findings.matters: This is a material, structural, recurring unfunded obligation that persists regardless of economic conditions, consuming 46% of the annual anti-poverty budget
findings.figures: notional 2026/27 CTS funding £21.787m vs actual cost £42.789m; caseload 46,881 (15,401 pension-age, 31,480 working-age)
findings.quote: the notional 2026/27 CTS funding from Government is estimated at £21.787m, while the cost of the scheme is £42.789m, which means the Council is subsidising the scheme by £21.002m based on claimants as at 30 June 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Major leadership restructuring in Adult Social Care and health partnerships during 2025/26
findings.detail: Both the Manchester Local Care Organisation and Adult Social Care senior teams underwent significant restructures with several retirements during 2025/26. These changes were completed by April 2026 but required re-establishment of relationships between newly appointed senior leaders.
findings.matters: Leadership transitions in major service areas can create continuity risk, knowledge loss, and decision-making delays that affect financial management and service stability.
findings.figures: Changes completed by April 2026
findings.quote: 2025/26 has been a period of transition, with changes across both the LCO and Adult Social Care (ASC) senior teams due to restructures and several retirements. ... These substantial organisational changes were completed by April 2026, enabling the re-establishment of new senior relationships required to drive shared priorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing maintenance insourcing project planned over 18 months with Equans contractor
findings.detail: The council is bringing housing maintenance functions in-house from an external contractor over the next 18 months. This is listed as a governance action requiring oversight of 'priorities and plans for the safe, secure and cost-effective insourcing of appropriate functions.'
findings.matters: Large in-sourcing projects carry cost and delivery risks that can lead to budget overruns or service disruption; the emphasis on 'cost-effective' execution suggests financial scrutiny is needed.
findings.figures: Timeline: 18 months
findings.quote: Housing maintenance insourcing (Equans) – governance of priorities and plans for the safe, secure and cost-effective insourcing of appropriate functions over the next 18 months.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Adult Social Care functions returning to council from Greater Manchester Mental Health Trust in October 2026
findings.detail: Functions currently delegated to GMMH are due to return to direct council management in October 2026. The AGS identifies the need for effective governance and assurance mechanisms before, during and after this transition, suggesting it is a complex operational and potentially financial transfer.
findings.matters: Major service transitions create operational and financial risk; if the return is poorly managed or funded, it could create budget pressures or service delivery failures affecting council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Return date: October 2026
findings.quote: Effective governance and assurance mechanisms for the delivery of currently delegated Adult Social Care functions to Greater Manchester Mental Health Trust (GMMH) before, during and following the return of these functions to the Council (due October 2026)

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Council's low council tax base identified as high risk in CIPFA Financial Resilience assessment
findings.detail: The Financial Resilience Index shows Manchester to be relatively well placed on earmarked reserves, but the only ratio classed as high risk is the low council tax base. The council is attempting to mitigate this through growing other income streams and advocating for council tax equalisation in government funding discussions.
findings.matters: A low tax base constrains the council's financial flexibility and ability to self-fund services or manage emergencies, directly affecting creditworthiness and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Relatively well placed on earmarked reserves, reasonably comfortable mid position on other reserves. Only one CIPFA ratio classed as high risk: the tax base.
findings.quote: The only ratio classed as high risk relates to the low council tax base, which is well understood. This is mitigated by attempts to grow other income streams and highlighting the importance of council tax equalisation in all funding discussions and consultation with the government.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council breached prudential indicator for portfolio maturity profile; requested amendment to prudential limit
findings.detail: Council breached lower limit for expected maturity profile of portfolio maturing beyond 10 years, with actual position approximately 28% versus required 30%. Breach reflects short-term nature of borrowing undertaken in the year. Council requested amendment to limit within Capital Monitoring report to Executive.
findings.matters: Indicates short-term borrowing strategy is pressing against prudential control limits; amendment request suggests framework may be inadequate for current strategy
findings.figures: Portfolio maturity over 10 years: actual approximately 28% versus required 30%; amendment to 20% requested
findings.quote: There was a minor breach against one of the indicators, specifically the lower limit of the expected maturity profile of the portfolio maturing in over 10 years' time, which is c. 2% lower than the limit set. This reflects the short-term nature of the borrowing undertaken in the year, and a request to amend to 20% was included within the Capital Monitoring report to Executive in February.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council has extremely limited capacity to fund additional capital schemes from own resources
findings.detail: Capital financing reserve forecast shows declining balance over the medium term. While the existing approved capital programme remains affordable, the council explicitly notes minimal headroom for new capital schemes without either additional external borrowing or budget reductions.
findings.matters: Limits the council's ability to respond to new capital priorities or emergency needs; any new capital spending will require further debt or service cuts
findings.figures: Capital financing reserve forecast to decline substantially from £102.8m by 2030-31 based on existing approved programme
findings.quote: The graph highlights that the existing programme remains affordable within existing and forecast market conditions, but that there is extremely limited capacity to fund additional capital schemes using Council resources.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital financing reserves declining as council draws down to fund budget gaps; £102.8m reserves forecast to deplete
findings.detail: Capital financing reserves stood at £102.8m as at 31 March 2026. The council will draw transfers to fund gap between budget and actual costs: £5.0m in 2026-27, rising to £8.7m in 2027-28 and £15.8m in 2028-29. Chart shows reserves depleting substantially over the medium term.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves erodes financial flexibility and indicates cost growth is outpacing budgeted amounts, reducing buffer available for unexpected pressures
findings.figures: Starting reserves £102.8m; forecast transfers of £5.0m (2026-27), £8.7m (2027-28), £15.8m (2028-29)
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Reserves were £102.8m as at 31 st March 2026. The transfers noted above are expected to contribute to that balance falling

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Forecast interest expenditure rising from £70.3m to £82.7m by 2028-29; growth exceeds budget increases
findings.detail: Capital financing costs are growing due to persistently high interest rates and the historic capital investment programme. Interest expenditure alone forecast to grow 18% from £70.3m (2026-27) to £82.7m (2028-29). The total capital financing budget grows only 17% over the same period, indicating cost growth outpacing budget growth.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs consume an increasing share of revenue budget, reducing financial flexibility and ability to fund service delivery
findings.figures: Interest expenditure forecast £70.3m (2026-27), £75.9m (2027-28), £82.7m (2028-29); total capital financing budgets £54.1m, £60.4m, £63.2m
findings.quote: There is growth in this budget forecast in the medium-term financial plan, recognising the prevailing economic environment specifically significant construction inflation and interest rates at a persistently high level.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: LOBO lender triggered rate increase of 297 basis points in March 2026; £260m LOBO debt at ongoing refinancing risk with next call date September 2026
findings.detail: In March 2026, one LOBO lender exercised their option and increased interest rate from 4.50% to 7.47% on a loan with 28 years remaining. The council holds approximately £260m LOBO debt. The next LOBO option date is September 2026 covering approximately £30m. The council managed the March event through short-term borrowing but faces ongoing refinancing risk.
findings.matters: LOBO loans expose the council to lender-initiated refinancing at potentially unfavorable rates; the £260m exposure is material and the September call date is imminent
findings.figures: 297 basis point increase (4.50% to 7.47%), £260m total LOBO debt, £30m at September 2026 option date, 28 years remaining term on March 2026 refinancing
findings.quote: In March 2026 one lender exercised their option and increased the interest rate on one loan by 297 basis points from 4.50% to 7.47%...The Council holds c. £260.0m of LOBO debt...The next LOBO call option date in the Council's debt portfolio is September 2026 and covers c. £30.0m of debt.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council debt increased by £106.7m to £1,715.4m in 2025-26
findings.detail: PWLB medium-term borrowing of £115.0m and temporary borrowing from other local authorities of £42.4m increased total debt, partially offset by market loan repayment of £50m. The increase reflects borrowing required to fund the capital programme in a higher interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Growing debt levels increase the council's debt service burden and constrain future borrowing capacity and financial flexibility
findings.figures: £106.7m increase, £1,715.4m total debt, £115.0m PWLB borrowing, £42.4m temporary borrowing from other authorities
findings.quote: The Council has increased borrowing by c. £106.7m to c. £1,715.4m during the year. PWLB medium term borrowing of £115.0m and additional medium term temporary borrowing from other local authorities of £42.4m increased total debt, and there were repayments of one Market Loan of £50m

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Assurance Opinion and Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Adults Services undergoing significant senior leadership restructuring concurrent with major operational transformation programmes
findings.detail: Adults Services is in a period of change with new Strategic Director, Director of Operations and Director of Commissioning and Transformation. Alongside this, two major programmes are underway: refresh of the Section 75 agreement with Manchester Foundation Trust (Local Care Organisation) and insourcing of Mental Health Strategic Duties from Greater Manchester Mental Health Trust due September 2026. The latter involves transfer of staff from GMMH back into the Council alongside related statutory duties. Both require clear governance and oversight.
findings.matters: Leadership transitions combined with major operational changes present execution risk. The timing of personnel changes alongside statutory duty transfers creates potential for governance gaps, service disruption, or incomplete integration. Staff transfers and contractual changes also carry financial and liability implications.
findings.figures: Mental health services insourcing due completion September 2026
findings.quote: Adults Services are in a period of change and restructuring at a senior level with a new leadership team, including a new Strategic Director, Director of Operations and Director of Commissioning and Transformation. Alongside this strategic change there are key operational programmes of work that are being delivered including the refresh of the Section 75 agreement with Manchester Foundation Trust around the work of the Manchester Local Care Organisation and the insourcing of the City Councils Mental Health Strategic Duties from the Greater Manchester Mental Health Trust (GMMH) which is due for completion in September 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Assurance Opinion and Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Five critical or significant audit recommendations remain outstanding past their due date
findings.detail: Of 57 critical or significant priority recommendations being tracked, 5 were outstanding past their due date as of 31 March 2026. While 43 have been confirmed as fully or partially implemented, the overdue recommendations indicate challenges in implementing audit findings. This includes unresolved issues across Adults (3), Corporate Services (1), and Neighbourhoods (1).
findings.matters: Overdue audit recommendations suggest slower-than-planned management action on identified control weaknesses. Five overdue critical/significant items indicate potential governance implementation gaps that have not been resolved.
findings.figures: 5 outstanding recommendations past due date out of 57 total critical/significant recommendations; 43 fully or partially implemented; 9 not yet due
findings.quote: There were 57 critical or significant priority recommendations being tracked by Internal Audit at 31 March 2026. Of these 9 were not due and 43 had been confirmed as fully or partially implemented. There were 5 outstanding recommendations past their due date.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Assurance Opinion and Report 2025/26
findings.headline: People & Money system replacement delayed and faces cost escalation and benefits realisation risks
findings.detail: The replacement of the legacy SAP finance and human resources system with the new People & Money platform has experienced necessary delays, with go-live moved to mid-year cut-over. The council is adopting an 'adopt not adapt' approach which creates modernisation opportunities but carries risks if operational requirements are not clearly defined. As an early adopter of new software, the council faces implementation and system maturity risks. Extended delivery timeline introduces risks around cost escalation and benefits realisation if not tightly managed.
findings.matters: Major system replacements carry execution risk. Cost escalation and programme drift could add material expense. Unclear benefits realisation in a core financial system could affect financial controls and reporting.
findings.figures: No specific cost figures disclosed in this report
findings.quote: There have been necessary delays in the planned go live of People & Money with improvement moved to a mid-year planned cut-over. This extended delivery timeline supports more comprehensive testing and change communication, which is positive, but also introduces risks around cost escalation and benefits realisation if not tightly managed.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Assurance Opinion and Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account faces affordability challenges and significant regulatory and compliance risks
findings.detail: Housing services operates in a challenging regulatory environment with a Housing Regulator judgement of C2. Key risks identified include affordability of the housing revenue account itself, preparing for insourcing of a major housing repairs and maintenance contract, and ensuring compliance with Consumer Standards and health and safety requirements. Ongoing capacity challenges are noted as persistent.
findings.matters: The Housing Revenue Account is a major financial control. Affordability challenges directly threaten the council's ability to service housing debt and maintain housing stock. A regulator C2 rating indicates areas requiring improvement.
findings.figures: Housing tenancy fraud referrals increased 300% from 2024/25
findings.quote: There are ongoing significant risks for example around affordability of the housing revenue account; in preparing for the insourcing of a major housing repairs and maintenance contract; and ongoing work required to ensure compliance with Consumer Standards, repairs and health safety requirements which encompass the Council's legal requirements as a landlord.

findings.paper_title: Annual Internal Audit Assurance Opinion and Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Care package to payments process audit found only limited assurance over current arrangements in Adults Services
findings.detail: The audit of care package to payments in Adults Services was commissioned by the Interim Deputy Director and issued a limited assurance opinion recently. This audit reviewed processes and their impact on financial projections and financial reporting. A programme of improvement work is likely to follow. Limited assurance means the effectiveness of governance arrangements is questionable.
findings.matters: Limited assurance over payment processes in an adults services directorate that is managing care packages indicates potential gaps in financial accuracy and control. This directly affects both reporting integrity and the council's ability to track and verify expenditure.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion issued; specific remediation figures not quantified
findings.quote: A further programme of improvement work is also likely to follow the finalisation of our audit report on the care package to payments process. The audit was commissioned by the Interim Deputy Director of Adults to review processes and establish their impact on financial projections and financial reporting with a draft report issued recently providing only a limited assurance over current arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Audit Status Report - June 2026 - FINAL
findings.headline: Slow audit query responses and poor quality evidence delayed the 2024/25 audit
findings.detail: The lessons-learned section reveals that the council's finance team took several weeks to respond to some audit queries, and when evidence was provided, it was often of poor quality and did not fully answer the auditor's question. New audit team members did not follow established query protocols, and some emails were deleted, which slowed progress further. These process failures required a new document-sharing system (Signals) to be implemented for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Delayed and poor-quality responses to auditors indicate weak governance discipline and finance team capacity or capability issues. This kind of audit friction can slow the rebuild of assurance and may indicate deeper finance function problems.
findings.figures: Responses took several weeks in some cases
findings.quote: The audit team received all of the information requested in sufficient time to enable the audit opinion to be issued ahead of the deadline. However, there were some occasions where responses to queries took several weeks. In some cases, the evidence received was of poor quality and did not sufficiently answer the audit query.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Audit Status Report - June 2026 - FINAL
findings.headline: Casting errors (arithmetic mistakes) were found in the draft accounts submitted for audit
findings.detail: The lessons-learned section notes that during the 2024/25 audit, the finance team submitted draft accounts containing casting errors across the primary statements. These arithmetic errors had to be flagged by auditors and corrected by the council's finance team before accounts could be finalised. This signals a quality control gap in financial statement preparation.
findings.matters: Casting errors in financial statements indicate weak internal controls and quality assurance processes. They raise questions about the reliability of the council's finance function and whether other, non-obvious errors may exist in the numbers.
findings.figures: Multiple casting errors found across primary statements in 2024/25
findings.quote: There were some casting errors within the draft accounts across the primary statements which were flagged by the audit team and subsequently corrected by the Council's finance team.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Audit Status Report - June 2026 - FINAL
findings.headline: General ledger system migration in October 2026 will occur during the critical audit rebuilding period
findings.detail: The council plans to migrate to a new general ledger with a go-live date in October 2026, which falls within the 2025/26 audit period when the auditors are rebuilding assurance. The audit team will need to perform IT audit procedures, governance reviews, and data migration reconciliations to confirm the transfer is correct. Any migration failures could corrupt the financial records being audited.
findings.matters: A system migration during financial statement audit is a major operational risk. Failed data migration or incomplete transfer of financial records could corrupt the accounts or delay audit completion, potentially pushing back the path to an unmodified opinion.
findings.figures: October 2026 go-live date
findings.quote: The Council plans to migrate to a new general ledger, with a current 'go-live' date in October 2026. This is a significant operational change. Amongst other priorities, the Council will need to ensure that it has arrangements in place to secure the complete and accurate migration of data from the current system to the new system.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Audit Status Report - June 2026 - FINAL
findings.headline: Council will not receive an unmodified audit opinion until 2027/28 — a five-year audit weakness from 2023/24 onwards
findings.detail: Even after rebuilding assurance in 2025/26, the audit opinion will be qualified in both 2025/26 and 2026/27 due to lack of comparability with prior years. Only in 2027/28 will the council return to a clean, unmodified opinion. This extended period of compromised audit status is exceptional.
findings.matters: Five years of non-standard audit opinions indicates a severe and prolonged financial reporting crisis. Lenders typically require clean audit opinions; this trajectory suggests the council has fundamental financial control or reporting weaknesses.
findings.figures: 2025/26: qualified; 2026/27: qualified; 2027/28: unmodified
findings.quote: The audit team no longer needs to disclaim as it has regained assurance over the closing balance sheet. However, it qualifies all other primary statements due to a lack of assurance over the opening position which has the potential to impact the current year CIES, MIRS and Cash Flow.

findings.paper_title: Forvis Mazars Audit Status Report - June 2026 - FINAL
findings.headline: Two consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions mean the council's accounts have not been audited or verified
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimed opinion for 2023/24 (issued February 2025) and has also disclaimed 2024/25 because auditors lack assurance over opening reserves, which is fundamental to the accounts. This means the council's financial position has not been independently verified or guaranteed by auditors for two years running.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot assess credit risk without audited accounts. A disclaimed opinion signals financial reporting failure and governance breakdown. Without verified accounts, the council's actual financial position is unknown.
findings.figures: 2023/24 disclaimed February 2025; 2024/25 also disclaimed
findings.quote: We issued a disclaimed opinion on your financial statements for the 2023/24 financial year in February 2025. This meant we did not express an opinion on those financial statements, and as such we did not have assurance over the opening balances in the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: A taxation review has identified a potential £4.1m cost relating to the council's income stream treatment, creating balance-sheet risk
findings.detail: The council recognised a potential £4.1m cost following a review of taxation treatment of some income streams. No further detail is given on which income streams, what the issue is, or whether mitigation is available. This is a contingent liability that could affect balance sheet strength.
findings.matters: Hidden or uncertain tax liabilities create unquantified risk. A lender needs to know what this relates to and whether there is further exposure.
findings.figures: £4.1m potential cost
findings.quote: The Council has also recognised a potential £4.1m cost in the accounts following a review of taxation treatment relating to the some of the Council's income streams.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: Adults services bad debt provision increased by £4.9m due to reduced income collection as clients struggle with care costs
findings.detail: The council made an additional £4.9m provision for bad debts in Adults services, citing deterioration in income collection. The reason given is explicit: clients are struggling to pay for care costs as a result of the cost-of-living crisis. This signals both reduced income and increased need—clients cannot afford services but still need them.
findings.matters: A council's ability to collect its own income is a basic credit metric. A £4.9m deterioration in a single service in one year, driven by residents' inability to pay, signals both current cash-flow stress and risk that residents in future may be in even greater difficulty.
findings.figures: £4.9m bad debt provision increase
findings.quote: This year it has been necessary to make £4.9m available, largely to recognise a deterioration in the level of income collected in Adults services, as clients are struggling to pay for their costs of care, partially as a result of the cost of living crisis.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: Unachieved savings of £6.7m (23% of target), with pressure continuing in Children and Adults Services into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council set £28.8m of savings for 2025/26. Only £21.9m (77%) were achieved or mitigated; £6.7m (23%) was not. The unachieved savings were in Children Service placements (costs and demand higher than assumed), Adults Social Care (service redesign and income generation delays), Neighbourhoods (delays in advertising income scheme), and Growth and Development (income shortfall). The paper states these 'have been rectified as part of the budget process or are expected to be achieved in 2026/27'—but that assertion is unqualified.
findings.matters: Failed savings targets signal either unrealistic budget planning or poor control of spend. 23% failure is material. If these services could not deliver savings in 2025/26 despite planning, a lender must assess whether the 2026/27 mitigation is credible.
findings.figures: £28.8m savings target; £21.9m achieved (77%); £6.7m unachieved (23%)
findings.quote: Of these £21.9m (77%) have been achieved or mitigated, and £6.7m (23%) has not been achieved. The £6.7m relates to Children Service placements due to increase costs and demand; Adults Social Care due to service redesign and income generation; Neighbourhoods due to delays in implementing an advertising income scheme and Growth and Development unachieved income.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: HRA reserves drawn down £15.7m against planned £5.9m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The HRA planned to draw £5.9m from reserves to balance the year, but the actual drawdown was £15.7m—nearly triple the plan and £9.8m higher. The overspend was driven by property repairs, disrepair claims, fire risk assessment costs, and reduced heating income. The council explicitly states: 'Continued reserves draw down at this rate is not sustainable.' No mitigation plan is described.
findings.matters: The HRA cannot go into deficit; any shortfall must come from HRA reserves. At this drawdown rate, those reserves will be exhausted. The council has flagged the rate as unsustainable but does not describe corrective action, suggesting the underlying drivers (property condition, disrepair liability) may be structural.
findings.figures: Planned drawdown £5.9m; actual £15.7m; additional call £9.8m; total outturn drawdown 266% of plan
findings.quote: The 2025/26 HRA budget included a planned £5.9m draw down from HRA reserves to balance the annual HRA budget, however, the drawdown requirement was £15.7m, resulting in an additional £9.8m call on reserves. Continued reserves draw down at this rate is not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: DSG deficit now £59.2m cumulative, costing £2.4m per year in lost interest, with resolution uncertain beyond 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant ran £29.1m over in 2025/26, bringing the cumulative deficit to £59.2m. The council is financing this deficit from general fund, losing £2.4m in 2025/26 in interest that could otherwise be earned. Government has announced a SEND reform plan that could write off 90% (£51.9m for Manchester), but only if the council completes a Local SEND Reform Plan by June 2026 and only if the plan is agreed. The statutory override expires March 2028, leaving significant uncertainty about the remaining £5.8m and any future deficits.
findings.matters: A £59.2m liability with uncertain resolution is a structural balance-sheet risk for a lender. Even if 90% is written off, £5.8m remains and must come from General Fund, further depleting an already strained reserve. The paper notes this creates 'significant risk on the long-term viability of council's balance sheets.'
findings.figures: £29.1m 2025/26 in-year DSG overspend; £59.2m cumulative deficit; £2.4m lost interest in 2025/26; 10,002 EHCPs in place; potential write-off £51.9m (90%), leaving £5.8m residual
findings.quote: The 2025/26 in year position reports a £29.1m overspend, down £2.2m since the last report. This contributes to a cumulative DSG deficit position of £59.2m... Although this is welcome, the lack of certainty beyond 2028 introduces significant risk on the long-term viability of council's balance sheets and medium-term financial strategies.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £4.2m includes a 20% demand increase in learning disability services with rising complexity
findings.detail: The directorate reported a £4.2m overspend driven by rising activity across all care areas. Learning disability services saw a 20% increase in demand, contributing a £3.0m overspend. Complexity of care in residential, nursing and homecare packages added a further £2.7m pressure. These are active demand signals, not one-off items.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether social care overspends are cyclical or structural. A 20% rise in LD demand and rising complexity across all care types suggests structural cost pressure that budget-setting has not captured.
findings.figures: £4.2m Adult Social Care overspend; 20% increase in learning disability demand; £3.0m from complex LD services; £2.7m from complexity of care
findings.quote: The increase in complexity of care in residential, nursing and homecare packages contributes a £2.7m overspend to the position; with a £3.0m overspend on complex services relating to learning disability, which is displaying a 20% increase in demand this year, and in mental health services also due to increased demand and activity.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend of £11.2m is driven by LAC placements 23 above budget, costing 5% more per week than forecast
findings.detail: Looked After Children external residential placements ran 23 above the budgeted number, with average costs of £6,822 per week versus the budgeted £6,395—and 16 individual placements cost over £9,000 per week. The paper cites national placement sufficiency as a constraint, suggesting this is unlikely to reverse quickly.
findings.matters: Rising costs and demand in children's social care that the council cannot control signals ongoing budget pressure. The council achieved only £21.9m of £28.8m budgeted savings for the year, with £6.7m unachieved largely in Children Services.
findings.figures: 23 LAC placements above budget; £6,822/week actual vs £6,395 budgeted; 16 placements over £9,000/week; national average £6,000/week
findings.quote: The biggest pressure relates to external residential placements for Looked After Children (LAC) which are 23 above the number assumed at budget setting, up one placement since last reported. Costs of external residential placements are 5% higher than budget, with an average cost of £6,822 per week, compared to a budget of £6,395 and a national average of £6,000.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn Report to the end of March 2026
findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £4.2m will draw down the General Fund Reserve below prudent levels
findings.detail: The council overran budget by £4.2m in 2025/26. After the overspend, the General Fund Reserve falls to £25.1m. The council's own reserves strategy, approved in February 2026, recommends maintaining £30-35m as adequate. The council is planning a £7.5m top-up in 2026/27 just to return to that prudent range.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb financial shocks. Reserves already below target and actively declining signals limited buffer capacity.
findings.figures: £4.2m overspend; General Fund Reserve £25.1m; prudent range £30-35m
findings.quote: This will reduce to £25.1m after funding the overspend of £4.2m. As part of the 2026/27 budget setting process, Council approved a planned contribution to top up the general fund reserve by £7.5m to maintain the reserve at a prudent and reasonable level

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 25/26
findings.headline: Volatile financial markets and persistent inflation are increasing borrowing costs and creating sustained pressure on capital programme costs
findings.detail: The council reports 'financial markets that are proving volatile due to persistent inflation concerns and geopolitical events', putting 'pressure on both the supply chain and interest rates, creating cost increases in both raw materials and labour but also the cost of financing capital expenditure'. The Bank of England has 'warned of additional inflationary pressures for the economy in the immediate future'. Construction inflation has not fully abated despite falling from peak levels.
findings.matters: Continued market volatility and inflation threaten to increase both capital project costs and debt financing costs beyond current forecasts, potentially forcing further programme reprofiling or cuts
findings.figures: CPI 3.3% (March 2026, down from peak 11.1% in Oct 2022); £30.0m unallocated inflation budget; £106.7m external debt borrowed in 2025/26 for 'relatively short durations' due to cost spikes
findings.quote: Geopolitical events continue to put pressure on both the supply chain and interest rates, creating cost increases in both raw materials and labour but also the cost of financing capital expenditure. Although inflation has fallen from peaks earlier in the decade, the impacts of a sustained inflationary period can still be seen in the construction sector, and the Bank of England has warned of additional inflationary pressures for the economy in the immediate future

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 25/26
findings.headline: Large capital programme creates significant future revenue budget commitments from debt financing and asset management that must be funded from constrained resources
findings.detail: The report explicitly warns that 'the significant size of the capital programme and level of borrowing required to fund its delivery, creates a significant future revenue budget commitment to both finance and repay the borrowing but also manage and maintain the assets created'. The Our Town Hall refurbishment alone exemplifies this risk. The council notes 'capacity for new schemes is limited' despite the large programme.
findings.matters: Revenue budget pressure from capital financing constrains the council's ability to deliver services and fund social care; large future liabilities reduce financial resilience
findings.quote: The significant size of the capital programme and level of borrowing required to fund its delivery, creates a significant future revenue budget commitment to both finance and repay the borrowing but also manage and maintain the assets created

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 25/26
findings.headline: General Fund Capital Financing Requirement breached by £24m due to higher-than-forecast homeless accommodation leases
findings.detail: Three prudential indicators have been breached. The General Fund CFR is £24m higher than forecast, 'which is predominantly due to the quantum of leases entered into to support homeless residents into temporary accommodation being higher than forecast a year ago'. The financing costs indicator is also higher than forecast because the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forced the council to use cash reserves rather than invest, reducing investment income.
findings.matters: CFR breaches signal unplanned increases in debt; homeless accommodation demand exceeding forecast suggests ongoing service pressure, and DSG deficit creating secondary revenue impacts on investment income
findings.figures: General Fund CFR £24.0m higher than forecast; overall CFR £0.3m higher; estimated financing costs to net revenue stream also higher than forecast
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirements for the General Fund and overall have been breached, which is predominantly due to the quantum of leases entered into to support homeless residents into temporary accommodation being higher than forecast a year ago

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 25/26
findings.headline: Expected capital receipts are being delayed and reduced in value due to interest rate impacts on property financing markets
findings.detail: The council notes that 'current market conditions, with interest rates higher than anticipated, have disrupted the market for financing land transactions', with 'some expected capital receipts are likely to be delayed or be reduced in value'. Several receipts that were expected in 2025/26 'did not progress as expected'. The future 3-year programme depends critically on £117.5m of capital receipts; if these do not materialise, 'the programme will need to be either be refinanced, reprofiled or reduced'.
findings.matters: A £1.092bn multi-year capital programme is dependent on receipts that are now proving unreliable; shortfalls force either programme cuts or increased borrowing (driving up debt service costs)
findings.figures: £87.7m carried forward from 2024/25; £56.7m received in 2025/26; £98.1m committed to future programme (£97.7m housing-related)
findings.quote: current market conditions, with interest rates higher than anticipated, have disrupted the market for financing land transactions. This means some expected capital receipts are likely to be delayed or be reduced in value

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: £200m ten-year borrowing commitment to fund capital programme, dependent on sustained 1% rent uplift
findings.detail: The council is committing to a 1% rent increase above CPI annually until 2034-35 (or 2036, depending on interpretation of the text). This secures £200m in borrowing capacity over the decade to fund £55m per annum capital investment (Asset Management, fire safety, decarbonisation, Collyhurst regeneration). This borrowing locks in multi-decade debt service obligations.
findings.matters: A ten-year borrowing commitment at fixed income growth creates budget rigidity. If repairs or compliance costs continue to rise faster than inflation, capital investment will be crowded out by debt service.
findings.figures: £200m borrowing over 10 years (CPI+1% on rents); £55m per annum reinvestment target; £110.7m net HRA debt already outstanding; CFR forecast £308.6m
findings.quote: The extra 1% uplift above CPI will be earmarked for additional borrowing, to enable significant capital investment to maintain decent homes standards, enhance fire safety, and tackle damp and mould issues, with the drawdown aligned to the Council's capital strategy.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: Of 76 councils surveyed in 2024/25, 93% reported HRA financial stress with 67% forecast in deficit from 2029/30 onwards
findings.detail: Manchester's position reflects a systemic HRA problem across England. Of 76 councils surveyed in 2024/25, 93% reported financial stress in their HRA, and 67% forecast to be in deficit from 2029/30 onwards. The survey predicts conditions will worsen further with continued inflation.
findings.matters: Widespread sector stress narrows policy solutions available to any single council and signals a structural housing finance crisis, not temporary pressure.
findings.figures: 93% of 76 responding councils in financial stress; 67% forecast deficit from 2029/30 onwards
findings.quote: In the 2024/25 Survey, of the 76 Local Authorities who responded 93% indicated that their HRA was in financial stress, with 67% being in financial deficit from 2029/30 and this is only likely to be exacerabted after a further 12 months of inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: £24m Residual Liabilities Reserve—untouched since before 2010—now deployed to fund two years of deficits
findings.detail: A reserve established before 2010 and held at £24m for 15+ years with no calls is now proposed for deployment to cover the 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits. The drawdown funds fire risk assessments (£2.4m), disrepair backlog (£2.4m), specialist repairs, waking watch costs, and insourcing setup (£3.5m). Once consumed, only the dwindling general reserve remains.
findings.matters: Deploying a long-protected reserve signals the severity of the budget crisis and removes a buffer. The council is now effectively single-reserve dependent, with accelerated depletion likely.
findings.figures: £24m reserve active since pre-2010; proposed total drawdown 2026/27–2027/28 £14.6m; £3.5m for insourcing infrastructure
findings.quote: It is therefore proposed that this reserve is utilised to support the recovery plan and fund the planned deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, as well as the one off costs of providing the main repairs and maintenance services in house.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: Manchester holds 212 empty council homes with target reduction to 90 by June 2026; only 8% returned within standard 21-day period
findings.detail: Manchester currently holds 212 vacant properties (212 out of ~15,000 stock is 1.4%). Only 8% of void properties are returned to tenancy within the standard 21-day target, indicating a severe processing backlog. The council has revised its target to reduce voids to 90 by June 2026.
findings.matters: Empty properties generate zero rent while requiring maintenance spending. Slow void turnaround directly reduces revenue and worsens the deficit. A void rate running above the 1% target is itself a cost pressure.
findings.figures: 212 council homes currently empty; target reduction to 90 by June 2026; only 8% returned within standard 21-day period
findings.quote: with 212 council homes currently empty. The revised target is to reduce this to no more than 90 by June 2026; currently, only 8% of voids are returned within the standard 21‑day period.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: Recovery plan contains unfinalized workstreams and is missing detailed costing and timelines
findings.detail: The sustainability plan to close the £14.9m annual deficit relies on eight workstreams. Multiple workstreams show 'TBC' (to be confirmed) status with savings not yet quantified: resourcing review, income generation initiatives, and PFI commercial review. The detailed repairs recovery plan is due end of February 2026. Plans are described as 'still to be finalised'.
findings.matters: A recovery plan with significant savings targets unspecified creates execution risk. If identified measures cannot be delivered, the deficit persists and reserves continue draining.
findings.figures: £3.724m savings needed 2026/27, £5.303m in 2027/28, £5.881m in 2028/29; multiple workstreams listed 'TBC' with no value assigned
findings.quote: For each of the workstreams identified, a project plan with the associated timeline being developed for the actions needed. Details around further mitigating actions are still to be finalised and will enable the accelation of the financial recovery.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: Repair costs have exploded 122% in five years; disrepair claims jumped from £19k to £5.1m in two years
findings.detail: Main repairs contractor costs rose from £11.5m (2021/22) to £25.6m (2025/26 forecast). Disrepair claims—tenant compensation for poor housing—surged from £19k in 2023/24 to £5.061m in 2025/26 forecast. The Regulator noted the repairs service has been underperforming with satisfaction below target.
findings.matters: The repairs cost spiral is the primary driver of the deficit and is structural, not cyclical. Escalating disrepair claims indicate building condition issues and unquantified legal exposure.
findings.quote: Repair costs, there has been a 122% in repair costs over the past five years. Rapid growth in disrepair claims, projected to cost £5.061m in 2025/26, compared with £3.795m in 2024/25 and £19k in 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA forecast £14.9m deficit in 2025/26; general reserves projected to run out by 2027/28 without recovery action
findings.detail: The 2025/26 HRA deficit is forecast at £14.9m, more than double the budgeted £5.9m drawdown. This represents 15% of HRA income. General reserves will fall to £17m by end-2025/26 and are projected to run out entirely by 2027/28 if no recovery action is taken. Minimum safe reserves are estimated at £10.5m (10% of income).
findings.matters: A council depleting reserves to cover operating losses cannot maintain capital investment or respond to emergencies. Reserve exhaustion forces service cuts or unplanned borrowing.
findings.figures: £14.9m forecast overspend 2025/26; general reserves fall from £32m (2021/22) to £17m (end 2025/26); exhausted by 2027/28 without action
findings.quote: The £14.9m deficit represents c15% of income generated and is unsustainable. The budget needs to be restructured to align expenditure with the income available.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Discretionary capital schemes only approved if they are fully externally funded, generate receipts, or deliver clear revenue savings
findings.detail: Section 5.6 sets out that additional borrowing 'will only be considered if there are no other funding available and the project is of critical importance.' This reveals the council believes it has reached limits on how much more it can prudently borrow. Schemes now face a strict financial gate: external grant, asset sales revenue, or invest-to-save only.
findings.matters: This signals the council's own finance officers believe borrowing headroom is exhausted for non-critical investment. New demands (service failures, statutory compliance, emergency repairs) would require either revenue cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £5m annual invest-to-save delegation ceiling (Section 10.11)
findings.quote: Additional borrowing will only be considered if there are no other funding available and the project is of critical importance. The impact on the Council's revenue budget will form part of the decision making

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting will increase recorded debt on balance sheet; final figures still uncertain
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 means most leases are now recorded as liabilities on the balance sheet (previously off-balance-sheet). This increases measured debt without changing actual cash outflows. However, Section 11.4 warns the audited lease figures for the 2024/25 accounts are still not finalised and 'may require a future revision' to prudential indicators.
findings.matters: A lender using balance-sheet debt ratios will see a step-change increase in reported leverage. The uncertainty about final lease figures creates risk that prudential indicators may be breached or revised.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 impact unquantified in this document
findings.quote: Whilst the audit process for the 2024/25 year remains ongoing, there remains a risk that the figures incorporated in the prudential indicators for leases may be subject to change, and may require a future revision to the indicators

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: HRA has to balance statutory/safety compliance with affordability; borrowing expanding
findings.detail: The HRA faces competing demands for limited capital: health and safety compliance, Decent Homes Standard, zero carbon targets, and new housing. Section 8.1 frames this as tension between 'regulatory and statutory requirements' and affordability. They are increasing HRA borrowing (£95.7m of the £509.3m total) and relying on 1% rental increases above inflation to fund it.
findings.matters: If rental income does not materialise as forecast (void rates, tenant arrears, or political pressure to freeze rents), the HRA's ability to service new debt becomes constrained. HRA viability is load-bearing for the whole council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £95.7m HRA borrowing planned; HRA capital programme £218m across 2025/26 to 2028/29
findings.quote: There are several competing investment demands for the HRA which need to be prioritised, from regulatory and statutory requirements such as health and safety compliance and the Decent Homes Standard to investment to meet the Council's zero carbon ambition

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Construction costs and financing costs remain high with no relief expected soon
findings.detail: The council has revised its capital programme because historical cost inflation and interest rates have not fallen as previously forecast. Section 5.5 explicitly cites 'increased construction and financing costs' as the driver for budget revisions. These remain sustained challenges with no obvious end date.
findings.matters: A lender funding projects at fixed rates will face pressure if construction outturn costs exceed contract prices. The council's ability to cover overruns from revenue is limited.
findings.figures: Construction inflation and interest rates 'historically high'; 'persistently high' interest rates noted
findings.quote: The volatility in inflation and financial markets has led to increased construction and financing costs, and interest rates have not fallen as has been forecast over the last couple of years

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: 15% of the five-year capital programme depends on capital receipts from asset sales whose valuations and timing are uncertain
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £157.9m from capital receipts (sale of surplus assets) to fund the programme. Officers explicitly state these forecasts 'cannot be certain and are therefore subject to change.' If actual sale proceeds fall short, 'the programme would need to be reviewed.' No contingency appears to be built in.
findings.matters: A commercial property downturn or slower-than-expected asset disposals would force unplanned cuts to the capital programme or require additional borrowing. This is a material execution risk on the whole strategy.
findings.figures: £157.9m from capital receipts (15% of total £1,022.6m programme)
findings.quote: Whilst the forecasts for future receipts are prudent, and based on the current expectations, they cannot be certain and are therefore subject to change. The implication of this is that, whilst the programme is forecast to be funded, should actual receipts fall below current expectations the programme would need to be reviewed

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital spend profile is explicitly acknowledged as highly ambitious and at delivery risk
findings.detail: Officers admit the forecast for next year is unrealistically aggressive given current market conditions. Delays to phasing are expected due to supply issues, inflation, and labour shortages. The provisional spend profile may not materialise, meaning actual capital receipts drawn will be lower than budgeted.
findings.matters: If the council cannot spend as fast as planned, capital receipts revenues and RCCO timing will miss. Revenue reserves may be drawn to cover financing costs on unspent borrowing.
findings.figures: £461.4m forecast for 2026/27
findings.quote: the phasing of schemes will be impacted by market challenges and, in the context of a challenging delivery market, particularly due to supply issues and inflation. On a project-by-project basis there will be optimism bias with regards to how quickly managers assess that projects will progress and be delivered, which means that the forecast for 2026/27 is highly ambitious

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Interest rate rises have blown the financing budget forecast
findings.detail: The council budgeted for interest rates to fall, but rates have remained persistently high. This forced an upward revision to the capital financing budget within the MTFP to keep the programme affordable. The revenue side is absorbing higher-than-expected debt service costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's revenue budget is tightening under financing pressure, and whether future rate rises could force further programme cuts.
findings.figures: £509.3m borrowing over 2025/26 to 2029/30 (50% of funding)
findings.quote: interest rates have not fallen as has been forecast over the last couple of years. To recognise this, additional funding is being allocated to the capital financing budget within the proposed MTFP

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: Council tax base is structurally weak compared to English average, limiting revenue-raising flexibility
findings.detail: Council tax makes up only 31.9% of Manchester's CSP in 2025/26, compared to a national average of 52.6%. Despite growth in house building (3,035 new dwellings in 2025/26), the council 'still has one of lowest levels of council tax as a proportion of core government funding in the country.' This structural constraint limits future revenue-raising options if grants decline or demand rises further.
findings.matters: Other councils can raise council tax to absorb shocks; Manchester cannot, because its base is low and residents have lower ability to pay. This makes it more dependent on grant funding, which is volatile.
findings.figures: 31.9% of CSP from council tax (vs. 52.6% national average); 3,035 new dwellings delivered in 2025/26
findings.quote: Despite the growth in house building in the city, the Council still has one of lowest levels of council tax as a proportion of core government funding in the country, making up only 31.9% of CSP in 2025/26, compared to a national average of 52.6%.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: Investment income from Manchester Airport Group shareholding has not recovered from pandemic and may not return to pre-2020 levels
findings.detail: The council earned £71m from shareholdings in 2019/20, but 'Income at this level is not expected to resume for some time.' Current contribution is only £12m annually (from loan interest to MAG). The budget relies on this £12m ongoing, but there is no recovery plan or trigger for reviewing if MAG can return capital or income.
findings.matters: A £59m gap between historic income and current reality is being absorbed by other sources (grant funding, council tax, reserves). If MAG income does recover, great; if it doesn't, it's a permanent loss of capacity. Lenders need to model the downside.
findings.figures: £71m earned 2019/20; £12m budgeted currently; £59m gap
findings.quote: In 2019/20, prior to the pandemic, the Council earned £71m from all of its various shareholdings. Income at this level is not expected to resume for some time. The interest from the loans to MAG advanced in 2018/19 and 2020/21 continue to contribute a net £12m each year

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: Balanced budget relies on £14.8m of value-for-money savings, with limited track record disclosed
findings.detail: The council proposes £14.8m of VFM and transformation savings in 2026/27 (Table 6), increasing to £20.3m by 2028/29. These include £6m of unallocated corporate items savings. The paper does not detail whether prior-year VFM targets were met, how embedded these savings are, or what the risk is if delivery slips.
findings.matters: Savings-dependent budgets are higher-risk in social care-heavy councils, where demand shocks are common. If £14.8m does not land, the buffer evaporates and a deficit appears.
findings.figures: £14.8m VFM savings in 2026/27; £20.3m by 2028/29; £6.0m unallocated (corporate items)
findings.quote: The current VFM measures, which scrutiny committees were asked to consider, amount to £14.8m in 2026/27, increasing to £20.3m by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: Significant capital borrowing programme (£383.9m) with no identified repayment plan in the document
findings.detail: The council is planning 'additional borrowing of £383.9m to 2028/29' to fund the Town Hall refurbishment, affordable housing, and capital priorities. The paper states that 'the Council must ensure its levels of long-term borrowing are proportionate to the size of the net revenue budget and are affordable, prudent and sustainable, in line with the CIPFA prudential code,' but does not set out the financing strategy or impact on future revenue.
findings.matters: £383.9m is material (37% of the net revenue budget). It will create ongoing financing costs. A lender needs to see that this borrowing is matched against revenue capacity and won't force future cuts.
findings.figures: £383.9m additional borrowing to 2028/29; net revenue budget £1.046bn
findings.quote: The capital programme, including the refurbishment of Our Town Hall as well as the need to deliver priorities such as affordable housing will require additional borrowing of £383.9m to 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: 100% business rates retention scheme ends in 2026/27, eliminating a major windfall income source
findings.detail: Manchester has benefited from retaining 100% of business rates growth above the government baseline since 2013. The council retained £122.8m to 2024/25 and forecast £35.7m more in 2025/26. However: 'The business rates system reset in 2026/27 recalibrates baselines to reflect actual rates income. At this point the benefit from the 100% scheme will tend to zero and grow over time in line with base growth.' This eliminates a major source of strategic flexibility that has been smoothing reserves and funding ongoing investment.
findings.matters: This is a structural revenue cliff — the council loses both the accumulated cushion and future growth windfalls from a scheme it has relied on for 14 years. It narrows future manoeuvre and makes future deficits harder to manage.
findings.figures: £122.8m retained to 2024/25; £35.7m forecast 2025/26; income 'tends to zero' from 2026/27
findings.quote: The business rates system reset in 2026/27 recalibrates baselines to reflect actual rates income. At this point the benefit from the 100% scheme will tend to zero and grow over time in line with base growth.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and 2026/27 Revenue Budget
findings.headline: Current-year social care overspend of £13m dragging into 2026/27 and beyond
findings.detail: Manchester is facing a £6.8m overall overspend in 2025/26, with £13m of that from Children's and Adults' Services combined. The council notes that 'these increasing pressures mean the budget demands in 2026/27, and beyond, will increase with the full year effect of the increased numbers of residents requiring care and support this year.' Table 5 shows social care growth (Children + Adults) of £13.1m in 2026/27 alone, rising to £21.2m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Current overspends indicate the budget assumptions may be optimistic; full-year carrythrough of demand growth is a known risk in every council. This is not a generic pressure — Manchester is naming specific live overspend.
findings.figures: £6.8m 2025/26 overspend overall; £13.0m social care element; £13.1m social care growth in 2026/27; £21.2m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The council is facing an overspend of £6.8m in 2025/26. The Social Care element of this is £13.0m across Children's and Adults' Services.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: Capital financing reserves being used to mitigate revenue budget impact, signalling budget pressure from debt costs.
findings.detail: The council has a capital financing budget of c. £45.6m p.a. to cover interest and MRP, and has been building this reserve from underspends created by internal borrowing savings. However, as external debt increases and internal borrowing falls, these existing capital financing reserves are being 'used to mitigate the impact on the capital financing revenue budget', indicating pressure on the revenue position from rising debt costs.
findings.matters: Using reserves to offset rising debt financing costs is unsustainable and signals the revenue budget will face growing pressure as reserves deplete.
findings.figures: Capital financing budget c. £45.6m p.a. net of investment income; reserves being drawn to mitigate cost increases
findings.quote: The Council has a capital financing budget, currently c. £45.6m p.a. net of investment income and increasing in future years, to fund interest costs and additional MRP. Any underspends against this budget are used to build up the Capital Financing and Capital Fund reserve... As the capital programme is reaching maturity and with the use of reserves increased, the level of external debt is increasing, with the existing capital financing reserves being used to mitigate the impact on the capital financing revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: HRA total external debt forecast £277.3m by 2028/29, with planned borrowing of £38.8m, £29.8m and £26.6m over three years
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is moving from a position where it took only £50m of borrowing since self-financing in 2012 to an explicit borrowing programme. HRA planned capital expenditure funded by borrowing is £38.8m (2026/27), £29.8m (2027/28), and £26.6m (2028/29). This will increase HRA total external debt from current levels to £277.3m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A step-change in HRA borrowing signals material shift in housing financing strategy and adds debt obligations that must be serviced from rental income within a ring-fenced account.
findings.figures: HRA total external debt forecast £215.6m (end 2026/27), £233.9m (end 2027/28), £277.3m (end 2028/29); planned borrowing £38.8m, £29.8m, £26.6m respectively
findings.quote: Since self-financing the HRA has only taken £50m of borrowing, which occurred in 2025/26, meaning the debt position has been relatively benign. However, as noted in the Capital Strategy elsewhere on this agenda, borrowing will form a key part of the funding for the future HRA programme.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting change adds uncertainty to debt figures, with 2024/25 audit still ongoing and risk of indicator revision.
findings.detail: The council implemented IFRS 16 (which treats most leases as balance sheet debt) for the 2024/25 accounts. This increased recognised debt liabilities correspondingly. However, the audit for 2024/25 is still ongoing, and the council explicitly notes there is a risk that lease figures may be subject to change and could require revision to the prudential indicators.
findings.matters: Unresolved accounting changes that increase reported debt create uncertainty over actual financial position and debt metrics used by lenders to assess risk.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 affects 2024/25 accounts onwards; audit still ongoing as of February 2026
findings.quote: Whilst the audit process for the 2024/25 year remains ongoing, there remains a risk that the figures incorporated in the prudential indicators for leases may be subject to change, and may require a future revision to the indicators.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast at £2.28bn (31 March 2026), with capital programme 'reaching maturity' but continued major investment.
findings.detail: Manchester's CFR is substantial at c. £2.28bn, driven by significant capital investment including the Town Hall refurbishment and highways maintenance funded by borrowing. The strategy notes the capital programme is 'reaching maturity', but new commitments including HRA housing investment mean the CFR will continue to grow to £2.49bn by 2026/27 and £2.52bn by 2027/28.
findings.matters: The scale of committed capital expenditure and continuing borrowing need defines the council's medium-term debt trajectory and interest cost burden.
findings.figures: CFR forecast £2.28bn at 31 March 2026; £2.49bn at end 2026/27; £2.52bn at end 2027/28
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement of the City Council as at 31st March 2026 is forecast to be c. £2.28bn... The capital programme for the next 3 years has been set... the Council will need to undertake external borrowing in the future and will not be able on to rely on internal borrowing alone.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: New external borrowing of £262m planned for 2026/27 as internal borrowing reserves deplete.
findings.detail: The council is forecast to require £262m of new borrowing in 2026/27, compared to £125.5m in the current year. This step-change reflects the council's strategy of maximising internal borrowing from reserves and cash, but as these are drawn down for capital and revenue spending, external debt will increase and interest costs will rise. The council has been internally borrowing (using own cash) to defer external debt, with c. £0.58bn of the CFR funded this way.
findings.matters: A significant increase in new borrowing and the depletion of internal reserves signals growing reliance on external debt markets and reduces financial flexibility for future shocks.
findings.figures: 2026/27 new borrowing £262.0m (up from £125.5m in 2025/26); internal borrowing c. £0.58bn
findings.quote: New Borrowing 125.5 [2025/26]... 262.0 [2026/27]... However, as reserves are used, either for capital or revenue spend, and as the CFR increases the level of external debt will increase, and therefore interest costs are likely to rise.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 26/27
findings.headline: £310m of LOBO loans (above 4% rate) create refinancing risk if interest rates stay elevated.
findings.detail: The council holds around £310m of Lender Option Borrower Option loans with interest rates above 4%. These give lenders the right to change rates on specific dates, and borrowers the right to repay if rates become unacceptable. Over the last decade only one lender has exercised this option, but if rates remain high or rise further, refinancing costs could increase significantly for the council.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk on a large portion of debt is material to lenders assessing the council's debt sustainability and budget resilience.
findings.figures: £310.0m of LOBO debt; existing rates above 4%
findings.quote: Around £310.0m of the outstanding debt consists of Lender Option Borrower Option (LOBO) loans. LOBO loans have options on specific dates that allow the lender to change the interest rate (the lender option), and the borrower can choose to accept the change or repay the loan if the new rate is unacceptable (the borrower option). The loans have interest rates above 4%, and therefore over the last decade only one lender has sought to exercise their option. However, there is a risk that should rates persist at relatively high levels or continue to rise, more lenders could seek to exercise the options, which would represent a refinancing risk to the Council where interest rates could increase on this proportion of debt.

findings.detail: Follow-up audit found two recommendations remain outstanding in full and three implemented only in part. findings.matters: Slippage on grant-funded capital programmes creates reputational risk with funders and suggests the council lacks capacity to deliver complex environmental initiatives.

findings.headline: Housing tenancy fraud caseload increased from 126 to 160 cases; four new investigators recruited
findings.detail: Housing tenancy fraud cases carried forward increased from 126 to 160 (42 new referrals received in Q3, only 8 closed). Allegations include false applications, right-to-buy abuse, subletting, and succession fraud.
findings.matters: Active fraud in social housing diverts scarce housing stock from genuine need and erodes control environment; significant caseload suggests systematic vulnerability.

findings.quote: Four of the postholders will focus on housing tenancy referrals and will be working alongside colleagues within Manchester Housing Partnership to help ensure that allegations regarding false applications for housing, right to buy discounts, succession applications and parting possession and sublet are fully investigated.

findings.headline: Housing repairs quality inspection programme remains unimplemented despite longstanding recommendation; March 2027 insourcing deadline creates delivery risk
findings.detail: A recommendation to implement post-inspection quality checks on housing repairs has remained outstanding for an extended period. A new Repairs Transformation Strategy has been approved with an explicit deadline of March 2027 for completing the service insourcing, but quality assurance is still not in place.
findings.matters: Lack of quality checks on a large repairs budget increases risk of defective work and tenant complaints; March 2027 insourcing deadline is aggressive given current control gaps.
